related_questions.question: What are the symptoms of a disease?

text_blocks.snippet: Symptoms are subjective experiences reported by an individual that can indicate a disease or condition. They are felt by the person experiencing them and are not directly observable by others. Common examples include pain, nausea, fatigue, and dizziness.
snippet_highlighted_words: subjective experiences reported by an individual that can indicate a disease or condition

list.title: Subjective Nature:
list.snippet: Symptoms are personal experiences, meaning they can only be described by the individual feeling them. For example, a headache or stomachache is a symptom because only the person experiencing it can report on it.

list.title: Contrast with Signs:
list.snippet: Symptoms differ from "signs," which are objective observations that can be seen or measured by others, like a rash or fever, according to EBSCO Research Starters.

list.title: Variability:
list.snippet: The same disease can manifest with different symptoms in different people, and some diseases may be asymptomatic, meaning they have no noticeable symptoms.

list.title: Examples:
list.snippet: Symptoms can range from mild and annoying to severe and debilitating, such as nausea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, shortness of breath, and fever, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Importance in Diagnosis:
list.snippet: While symptoms alone may not be enough to diagnose a disease, they provide crucial information for healthcare professionals to understand what might be happening in the body and guide further diagnostic testing, says the Cleveland Clinic.

text_blocks.snippet: The top 20 diseases, in terms of global mortality, include ischemic heart disease, stroke, lower respiratory infections, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and various cancers like lung and colorectal cancer. Other significant contributors to death are diabetes, Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, diarrheal diseases, and preterm birth complications.
snippet_highlighted_words: ischemic heart disease, stroke, lower respiratory infections, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and various cancers like lung and colorectal cancer

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed breakdown of some of the leading diseases:

list.title: Ischemic Heart Disease:
list.snippet: A leading cause of death globally, characterized by reduced blood flow to the heart.

list.title: Stroke:
list.snippet: Occurs when blood supply to the brain is interrupted, causing brain damage.

list.title: Hypertensive Heart Disease:
list.snippet: High blood pressure can lead to heart failure and other cardiovascular issues.

list.title: Lower Respiratory Infections:
list.snippet: Infections of the lungs and airways, including pneumonia, can be particularly dangerous for vulnerable populations.

list.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD):
list.snippet: A group of lung diseases that cause airflow blockage and breathing-related problems.

list.title: Cancer:
list.snippet: Various types of cancer, including lung, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancer, contribute significantly to mortality.

list.title: Diabetes:
list.snippet: A metabolic disorder that affects how the body uses glucose, leading to complications like heart disease and kidney failure.

list.title: Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias:
list.snippet: Progressive brain disorders that cause memory loss and cognitive decline.

list.title: Diarrheal Diseases:
list.snippet: Infections that cause severe dehydration, particularly dangerous for young children and the elderly.

list.title: Preterm Birth Complications:
list.snippet: Complications related to premature birth are a leading cause of death in infants.

list.title: Unintentional Injuries:
list.snippet: Accidents and injuries from various causes are also significant contributors to mortality.

list.title: COVID-19:
list.snippet: While mortality rates have declined, COVID-19 remains a major cause of death, particularly in certain regions.

list.title: Non-communicable Diseases (NCDs):
list.snippet: Heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases are largely driven by lifestyle factors, including diet, physical activity, and tobacco use.

list.title: Infectious Diseases:
list.snippet: While NCDs dominate, infectious diseases like HIV/AIDS, TB, and malaria remain significant health challenges, particularly in developing countries.

list.title: Environmental Factors:
list.snippet: Air pollution, access to clean water and sanitation, and other environmental factors significantly impact disease burden.

list.title: Socioeconomic Factors:
list.snippet: Poverty, lack of access to healthcare, and other socioeconomic disparities can exacerbate the impact of disease.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that the ranking of diseases can vary depending on the region, age group, and specific data source used.

text_blocks.snippet: Symptoms of a disease are the subjective experiences reported by a patient, while signs are objective, observable indicators of disease. Symptoms are what a person feels, like pain or fatigue, while signs are what a doctor might observe, like a fever or rash. Common symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, coughing, and digestive issues. Symptoms can vary greatly depending on the specific disease or condition.
snippet_highlighted_words: fever, fatigue, muscle aches, coughing, and digestive issues

list.snippet: Fever: An elevated body temperature, often a sign of infection.
Fatigue: Feeling unusually tired or lacking energy.
Muscle aches: Pain or soreness in the muscles.
Coughing: A reflex action to clear the airways, can be a symptom of various illnesses.
Digestive issues: Symptoms like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation.
Headaches: Pain in the head, which can be caused by various factors.
Skin changes: Rashes, itching, or other abnormalities on the skin.
Pain: Any kind of discomfort, from headaches to joint pain.
Shortness of breath: Difficulty breathing or feeling like you can't get enough air.
Changes in appetite: Loss of appetite or excessive hunger.
Chest pain: Can indicate heart problems or other conditions.
Abdominal pain: Can be a sign of digestive issues or other abdominal problems.
Swelling: Can occur in various parts of the body, often indicating inflammation.
Numbness or tingling: Can be a sign of nerve damage or other conditions.
Changes in vision: Blurred vision, double vision, or other vision problems.
Difficulty swallowing: Can indicate problems with the throat or esophagus.
Symptoms: are subjective and can only be reported by the person experiencing them.
Signs: are objective and can be observed by a healthcare professional.

text_blocks.snippet: A patient might report feeling a headache and fatigue (symptoms). The doctor might observe a fever (a sign) during the examination.

It's important to note that the presence of symptoms alone doesn't necessarily mean a person has a specific disease. It's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.
